 Nearly 22,000 workers in Wales set for pay rise as Living Wage increases
 By Rhys Gregory October 19, 2026 No Comments

 Nearly 22,000 people working for almost 650 real Living Wage employers in Wales are set for a pay rise after the voluntary real Living Wage went up to £14.10 an hour across the UK.
 The new rate, announced on Thursday 15 October, is an increase of 65p, or 4.8%.
 Employers in Wales signed up to pay the real Living Wage include Principality Building Society, Wealthify, and Wales and West Utilities. Recent accreditations in Wales include SWG Construction and Stage Goat Theatre Company.
 New figures show the campaign for a real Living Wage has secured nearly £5bn of pay rises for low paid workers around the UK since it began 25 years ago. Over £190m of that total is driven by employers in Wales.
 Living Wage Foundation analysis shows that a full-time worker earning the new real Living Wage would earn over £2,700 a year more than a worker earning the current government minimum. The foundation says this extra cash could cover eight months of food for a household or five months of housing and energy costs.
 First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: “I’m really pleased that the new real Living Wage is rising to £14.10 an hour in Wales. This is more than just a number – it’s about making sure workers are provided with security, dignity and a fair reward for their efforts.”
 “I commend the many employers in Wales that are already paying the real Living Wage. I encourage more employers to commit to paying the real Living Wage, which is good for their staff and their organisation.”
 Emily Cotterill, Head of Fair Economy at Cynnal Cymru – Wales Accrediting Partner for the Living Wage, said: “With nearly 650 Wales based employers paying the Living Wage, and many more Living Wage employers operating here in Cymru, today’s announcement will be felt across the whole nation. The Living Wage campaign is giving a pay rise to thousands of workers, supporting them, their families, and their local economies.”
 “We know that there is still more to be done to tackle in work poverty in Wales and the Living Wage Wales team are here to support employers wherever they are on their journey to becoming an accredited part of the Living Wage movement.”
 Despite the growth of the Living Wage movement, nearly 220,000 workers in Wales are paid below the real Living Wage, according to the foundation.
 Annie Davies, Managing Director at Fabulous Welshcakes, said: “At Fabulous Welshcakes, we’re committed to doing the right thing by our people, supporting our local community, and making responsible choices for the environment. Becoming a Living Wage employer has been a part of that journey. We have a brilliant team of around 30 people who all work hard to contribute to the success of the business. We think paying a wage that reflects the real living costs is the right thing to do.”
 “I think it helps our team to feel valued and recognised for the work that they do. We see that reflected in our retention rates within the business. We have found that people have stayed within our team for a long time, which is great and that has a knock-on effect because we spend less money on hiring and training new people as well.”
 Emily Sawh, Co-Director of the Living Wage Foundation, said: “Today’s increase to the real Living Wage will make a massive difference to hundreds of thousands of workers and their families up and down the country. They will be thousands of pounds better off this year thanks to the rise, helping them achieve the decent standard of living they need to thrive.”
 “Despite the Living Wage campaign’s monumental impact on wages in the UK, there are still millions of workers trapped in in-work poverty and struggling every day to make ends meet. They’re forced to skip meals, fall behind on bills and visit foodbanks. That’s why we urge employers to do the right thing by signing up to pay the real Living Wage and providing workers with the decent standard of living they need to thrive.”
 Across the UK, 1 in 7 employees now work for an accredited Living Wage Employer, and half the FTSE 100 are accredited Living Wage Employers.
 The real Living Wage is calculated by the Living Wage Commission and applies to all workers over 18. It is a voluntary scheme and is different to the Government’s National Living Wage, the legal minimum wage that all employers are required to pay, which is £12.71 as of April 2026 and applies to everyone over 21 years old.
